content: As an example, let $X = \lbrace A,B\rbrace $ , $Y_A = \lbrace \text{$a_{1}, a_{2}$, $a_3$}\rbrace $ , $Y_B = \lbrace \text{$b_1, b_2,$ $b_3$}\rbrace $ , and $k=3$ . Each $a_i$ and $b_i$ has 2 possible values, $a_{i1}$ or $a_{i2}$ and $b_{i1}$ or $b_{i2}$ respectively. Thus, mapping an input symbol to 48 ( $Y_A = \lbrace \text{$a_{1}, a_{2}$, $a_3$}\rbrace $0 ) possible permutations. A possible valid output for the input $Y_A = \lbrace \text{$a_{1}, a_{2}$, $a_3$}\rbrace $1 is $Y_A = \lbrace \text{$a_{1}, a_{2}$, $a_3$}\rbrace $2 . Note that such valid strings are selected at random when generating the dataset. We allow this stochasticity in the outputs in order to prevent the model from resorting to pure memorization. For our task, $Y_A = \lbrace \text{$a_{1}, a_{2}$, $a_3$}\rbrace $3 and each $Y_A = \lbrace \text{$a_{1}, a_{2}$, $a_3$}\rbrace $4 has a corresponding output alphabet $Y_A = \lbrace \text{$a_{1}, a_{2}$, $a_3$}\rbrace $5 of size 16.
